sections.heading: First Session: Clean, Collect, and Make Your First Sale
sections.intro: When you spawn into Sweep The Moon, the entire lunar surface is buried in space dust. Your job is to clean it one tile at a time, starting with nothing but a toothbrush. Walk up to any dust-covered tile and sweep, and the dust transfers into your canister. The starting toothbrush is slow and holds very little, which is the point: every upgrade you buy later makes the grind faster and more satisfying.
paragraphs: Once the canister is full, walk back to your base and empty it. The game converts that dust into cash on the spot. That cash is the only income source and the engine behind every progression decision. You can spend it on a better brush to sweep tiles faster, a larger canister to carry more dust per trip, or higher movement speed to cut the walk back and forth.

The overarching goal is to push the Moon to 100% clean, and you can bring up to three friends to cover more tiles at once. Sweep The Moon draws inspiration from Moon Sweepers on Steam, though the two share no confirmed mechanics.

sections.heading: Basic Controls and Interface
sections.intro: The core loop — sweeping tiles, filling your canister, and returning to base — is covered in the section above, so this section focuses on what you actually see and press on your first screen.
paragraphs: Sweep The Moon uses standard Roblox movement controls: WASD or the left thumbstick to walk, and your mouse or right thumbstick to aim the sweep direction. The sweeping action itself is triggered by clicking or pressing the action button while standing over a dusty tile. The on-screen canister meter fills as you collect dust, and an indicator at your base signals when it is ready to be emptied.

The main HUD displays your current cash balance, canister fill level, and a Moon cleanliness percentage. That percentage is the game's long-term progress tracker — the official goal is reaching 100% clean. Because the third-party source excerpt describes the game's flow rather than individual button bindings, exact keybind labels have not been independently confirmed; check the in-game Settings menu if you need a full control map.

sections.heading: Which Upgrade Should You Buy First?
sections.intro: Sweep The Moon offers three upgrade tracks: brush, canister, and speed. Brush upgrades let you sweep tiles faster or handle thicker dust layers. Canister upgrades increase how much dust you can hold before returning to the base. Speed upgrades reduce the time it takes to walk between tiles and back to the sales point.
paragraphs: For your first purchase, prioritize canister capacity if you find yourself making frequent trips to the base with only a few tiles worth of dust. A larger canister cuts down round-trip time and lets you clean more area per run. If your toothbrush feels slow on the tiles themselves, a brush upgrade will speed up the sweeping action. Speed upgrades become more valuable once you have a larger working radius and need to cover ground quickly.
Exact costs and stat increases are not documented in public sources. Check the in-game upgrade menu after your first sale to compare prices and decide which bottleneck to remove first.

sections.heading: Late-Session Goals: Vehicles, Automation, and Co-op
sections.intro: Once you can afford repeated brush and canister upgrades without waiting, you unlock three mid-game paths. The first is vehicles: drivable sweepers and giant rovers that cover far more ground per pass than any hand tool. The second is automation through buildable robots, conveyor belts, and processing machines that keep earning cash while you explore or plan your next expansion. The third is multiplayer — you can invite up to three friends into the same server and divide the remaining dirty tiles among your crew.
paragraphs: All three paths aim toward the same milestone: bringing the entire Moon surface to 100% clean. Check the Vehicles page for sweeper and rover comparisons, and see the Automation guide for robot and belt setup sequences.

The game confirms brush, canister, and speed upgrades as the first spending targets. Badges would likely mark your first upgrade purchase, first canister emptied, or a dust-volume threshold swept. The beginner guide page covers upgrade priority and first-session pacing in detail.

The mid-game shift to vehicles and automation opens drivable sweepers, giant rovers, and buildable systems — robots, belts, and machines. Each category represents a production-scale leap that badge systems reward: first vehicle driven, first robot deployed, or first automation loop closed. The vehicles page compares sweepers and rovers; the automation page explains how robots and belts form working setups.

The end-game milestone is the 100% clean Moon goal, designed for co-op groups of up to four players. Badges could track partial completion tiers — 25%, 50%, 75% — or team milestones such as a full four-player session or a personal dust total. This global objective gives badge designers a natural final-tier unlock once the community completes it or individual players hit verified thresholds.

paragraphs: Third-party player guides have started circulating online with claimed badge information, but these remain untested reports. Treat any badge claims from unofficial sources with caution until they match what the game actually displays in its own interface.

Sweep The Moon draws inspiration from Moon Sweepers on Steam, but that connection does not mean the two share badges, stats, or rewards. Steam achievement lists will not reliably predict what the Roblox version might add. The automation page covers more about how that inspiration relates to in-game mechanics.
